prompt: A request arrives with a valid token for Ana and asks for order 3, which is Bruno's. What has the API established so far?
hint: Two questions, asked in order.

choices.text: That Ana may read order 3, since her token is valid
choices.why: A valid token answers who is asking. Whether Ana may read this order is the second question, and it has not been asked yet.

choices.text: Who is asking, and nothing about what she may do
choices.why: Right. Authentication is done; authorisation has not started.

choices.text: Nothing yet, because a token proves nothing until the order is read
choices.why: The token is checked first and does prove something: that the request comes from Ana.

choices.text: That order 3 exists
choices.why: Nothing has looked at the orders yet, and in orders.py that check comes after the permission.

prompt: The shop's web page hides the refund button from customers. The refund route on the server checks that the token is valid and nothing more. What can a customer do?
hint: Every request in this course was typed with curl.

choices.text: Nothing, because the button is not there to press
choices.why: The button only sends a request. The same request can be typed without it.

choices.text: Only refund orders that are already their own
choices.why: Nothing on the server compares the order with the caller, so ownership is not checked either.

choices.text: Get a 401, because a customer's token is not accepted on that route
choices.why: The route accepts any valid token, a customer's included; that is the defect.

choices.text: Send the refund request with curl and have it succeed
choices.why: Right. Hiding is a convenience; the server has to decide on every request.

prompt: Put the checks a request to orders.py passes in the order they run.
hint: Who is asking comes before anything else is looked at.
items: Is the token one this API issued?
Is there a route for this address and method?
Is the route's permission in the caller's set?
Is this order one the caller may see?
Does the refund policy allow it today?
trap: Looking the order up before checking the token would answer a stranger differently for orders that exist.

prompt: Somebody adds a person with the role `auditor` to the database, and the code was never told about that role. What does each version of `allowed()` answer for `orders:refund`?
hint: One version lists refusals; the other lists grants.

choices.text: Both answer False, since neither function mentions the role
choices.why: Not mentioning the role is exactly what makes the refusal list answer True: it only refuses what it names.

choices.text: The refusal list answers True and the grant list answers False
choices.why: Right. The refusal list falls through to True; the grant list finds an empty set.

choices.text: Both crash with a KeyError
choices.why: The grant list uses `ROLES.get(role, set())`, which returns an empty set instead of raising.

choices.text: Both answer True, because a new role starts with every permission until somebody narrows it
choices.why: That would be allow by default. The grant list starts a role it does not know with nothing.

prompt: Complete the lookup so that a role missing from the table gets no permissions at all: `ROLES.get(role, ___)`
hint: An empty collection of the same type as the values.

prompt: A new row is added to `ROUTES` with the permission written as `order:read` instead of `orders:read`. What happens when people call it?
hint: Look for which role's set contains that string.

choices.text: It answers 404 for everybody, because the route is not registered
choices.why: The route is in the table and matches the address. It is the permission check that refuses.

choices.text: Everybody gets in, because a permission no role defines is not checked
choices.why: That would be the failure of a deny list. Here the string is looked for in the caller's set and never found.

choices.text: Everybody gets 403, and somebody notices on the first try
choices.why: Right. No set holds `order:read`, so the route fails closed and loudly.

choices.text: The server answers 500 with a KeyError
choices.why: Nothing looks the permission up as a key; it is tested with `in`, which answers False.

prompt: The shop wants a `support` role that can refund orders but cannot list people. In orders.py, what has to change?
hint: Where does a role mean anything in that file?

choices.text: One line in `ROLES`, and the people who get the role
choices.why: Right. The handlers ask about permissions, so none of them learns the new role exists.

choices.text: Every handler that checks for `staff`
choices.why: No handler checks for a role name. That is what checking permissions instead buys.

choices.text: A new row in `ROUTES` for each refund the support team will make
choices.why: Routes describe addresses, not people. The refund route already names `orders:refund`.

choices.text: The refund handler, to let `support` through
choices.why: The handler never sees a role; the dispatcher checks the permission before it runs.

prompt: Match each permission in orders.py to what it lets a caller do.
hint: One description belongs to no permission in the file.

pairs.right: read orders, as many as `find` allows
see every customer's orders, notes included

prompt: Dora is moved from `admin` to `staff`. In one API the role is read from a table on every request; in another it was copied into a JWT when her token was issued. When does each one stop letting her list people?
hint: What does each API believe, and until when?

choices.text: Both at once, on her next request
choices.why: The JWT still says `admin`, and the second API believes it without asking the database.

choices.text: Both when she signs in again
choices.why: The first API does not wait for anything: it reads the table on every request.

choices.text: The JWT one at once, since a signed token is checked every time
choices.why: The signature is checked every time, and it is still a valid signature over the old role.

choices.text: The table one on her next request; the JWT one when that token expires
choices.why: Right. A role inside a token is believed until the token ends; that is the price of not asking.

prompt: orders.py refuses a request with no token. Besides the 401 status, what does the answer carry that tells the client what to send?
hint: A header.

choices.text: A `Location` header pointing at a sign-in page
choices.why: `Location` is for a created or moved resource. An API answers 401 in place.

choices.text: An `Allow` header
choices.why: `Allow` lists methods, and comes with 405.

choices.text: `WWW-Authenticate`, naming a bearer token
choices.why: Right. `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="shelf"` says which kind of credential would do.

choices.text: A fresh demo token in the body, ready to be used on the next request
choices.why: Handing out tokens to whoever asks without one would make the check pointless.

prompt: Eva's role, `auditor`, is not in `ROLES`. Her token carries `orders:read`. What does `GET /orders` answer her?
hint: The effective set is what the role grants and the token carries.

choices.text: 200 with her own orders, because the token carries the scope
choices.why: A scope only counts where the role grants it too, and her role grants nothing.

choices.text: 401, because a role nobody defined makes the token invalid
choices.why: The token is one the API issued, so who is asking is answered. It is the second question that fails.

choices.text: 403, because her effective set is empty
choices.why: Right. An unknown role gives the empty set, and an empty set meets any scope in nothing.

choices.text: 500, from a KeyError on the unknown role
choices.why: `ROLES.get(role, set())` returns an empty set rather than raising.

prompt: Ana holds `orders:read` and asks for `/orders/3`, which is Bruno's. Which part of orders.py turns her away?
hint: The dispatcher let her in.

choices.text: The permission check in `dispatch`
choices.why: She holds `orders:read`, which is all the route asks for, so the dispatcher lets her through.

choices.text: `show`, which removes the fields she may not read
choices.why: `show` decides which fields go out, and only after the order was allowed. It never refuses one.

choices.text: The token check in `caller`, which ties each token to one customer's orders
choices.why: Tokens are tied to people, not to orders. That check only answers who she is.

choices.text: `find`, comparing the order's customer with the caller
choices.why: Right. The order is somebody else's and she lacks `orders:read_all`, so `find` returns None and she gets 404.

prompt: Which of these make an object-level flaw hard to write? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them is worth having and is still not the check.

choices.text: Looking every object up through one function that takes the caller
choices.why: Right. A handler cannot fetch an order without saying who wants it.

choices.text: Using random UUIDs in place of consecutive ids
choices.why: They make neighbours hard to guess, and an id still leaks through logs and links; then only the check is left.

choices.text: Filtering lists in the query by the caller
choices.why: Right. Somebody else's rows are never read at all.

choices.text: Testing with at least two people
choices.why: Right. A test that signs in as one person cannot ask for another's object.

prompt: You review `def get_invoice(self, me, perms, ident)`, which runs `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?` with `ident`, returns 404 when no row comes back and the row otherwise. The route requires `invoices:read`. What do you flag?
hint: Which argument does the handler never use?

choices.text: Nothing: the route permission already limits who can call it
choices.why: The permission says the caller may read invoices, not which ones.

choices.text: Any caller let through the route can fetch every customer's bill by trying other ids
choices.why: Right. `me` is never used, so nothing ties the invoice to the caller.

choices.text: The 404 should be a 403, so the caller knows the invoice exists
choices.why: Telling a stranger an invoice exists is the leak a 404 avoids. The missing piece is the owner check.

choices.text: `SELECT *` exposes columns; listing them would fix it
choices.why: Listing columns is a fix for which fields go out, not for whose invoice it is.

prompt: Bruno owns order 3, and his token carries `orders:refund`. What does `POST /orders/3/refund` answer him?
hint: Owning the order and being allowed the function are two questions.

choices.text: 200, since he owns the order and his token carries the scope
choices.why: Both are true and neither is enough: his role does not grant refunds.

choices.text: 403, from his role, which grants no refunds
choices.why: Right. Function-level authorisation refuses before ownership is even asked; the message is `the role customer lacks orders:refund`.

choices.text: 404, because a customer may not see refunds
choices.why: He can see order 3; it is his. The refusal is about the function.

choices.text: 403 with `insufficient_scope`, because the token is the half that refused
choices.why: His token carries the scope. It is the role that lacks it, and the answer says so.

prompt: Dora sends `DELETE /orders/3`. Why does orders.py answer 405 with `Allow: GET`, rather than a 501 page from Python's library?
hint: Look at the line after `dispatch`.

choices.text: Because an administrator's request is always answered by the API itself
choices.why: The role has nothing to do with it; a customer gets the same 405.

choices.text: Because the route table has a DELETE row that refuses
choices.why: There is no DELETE row. The 405 comes from finding the address with only a GET.

choices.text: `do_DELETE` is wired to `dispatch`, which finds no DELETE route there
choices.why: Right. Every method goes through the table, so the table is the whole list of what the API does.

choices.text: Because Python's library answers 405 for any method it was not told about
choices.why: It answers 501 for those, as lesson 1's OPTIONS showed.

prompt: Ana's order body names `status` and `total_cents` beside `book_id` and `quantity`. orders.py answers 422. Why refuse instead of storing the order and ignoring the two fields?
hint: What would the client believe afterwards?

choices.text: Ignoring them would store the status she sent
choices.why: Ignoring them keeps the status safe. The problem is what the client is left believing.

choices.text: The client would believe it had set a status that it had not
choices.why: Right. Refusing, and naming the fields, tells the client what was wrong.

choices.text: A 422 is required by HTTP for any unknown field
choices.why: HTTP requires no such thing; 422 is the code this course chose for content that breaks a rule.

choices.text: So that staff can set those fields in the same request
choices.why: Nobody sets them through this route; the server computes them.

prompt: Ana orders two copies of book 1, whose `price_cents` is 3990, and also sends `"total_cents": 1`. Leaving the refusal aside, what total does a correct server store, in cents?
hint: The server reads the price from the books table.

prompt: An API sends every column of the order as JSON, and the shop's page simply does not display `note`. Has a customer been shown the note?
hint: Where does the JSON end up?

choices.text: Yes; it reached their browser, and the developer tools show it
choices.why: Right. What the page does not display was still sent. Only the representation can leave it out.

choices.text: No, because a field the page does not draw is never received
choices.why: The page draws from what it received, and it received the whole row.

choices.text: No, as long as the request needed a valid token
choices.why: The token says who asked; it does nothing to the fields in the answer.

choices.text: Only if the customer owns the order
choices.why: Owning the order is why they received it at all. The note goes out with it either way.

prompt: In orders.py, what decides the permissions a request actually has?
hint: Python's `&` on two sets.

choices.text: What the role and the token both allow
choices.why: Right. The intersection: a token narrows, and never widens.

choices.text: The scopes on the token
choices.why: Bruno's token claims `orders:refund` and he still cannot refund. Scopes alone decide nothing.

choices.text: The role, with the token's scopes added to it
choices.why: Adding them would let a token widen what its owner may do.

choices.text: The role
choices.why: Ana's app token has her role and still cannot place an order.

prompt: When a request's role allows the action but its token's scope does not, orders.py answers 403 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="___"`.
hint: The name RFC 6750 gives this error.

prompt: To save a database query, a colleague proposes checking only the scopes a token carries and dropping the role lookup. With the six tokens of orders.py, what would change?
hint: Look for a token that claims more than its owner's role.

choices.text: Nothing, because every token carries exactly its owner's permissions
choices.why: Bruno's carries one more, and Eva's carries one her role does not grant.

choices.text: Ana's app could place orders
choices.why: Her app's token carries only `orders:read`. Scopes alone would still refuse it.

choices.text: Bruno could refund orders, and Eva could read hers
choices.why: Right. Both tokens claim a scope their role lacks, and only the intersection stopped them.

choices.text: Carla could list people
choices.why: Her token does not carry `people:read`, so scopes alone would refuse it as well.

prompt: `refund_order` refuses when `age > REFUND_DAYS`, and `REFUND_DAYS` is 30. What is the greatest age, in days, at which an order can still be refunded?
hint: Strictly greater than.

prompt: Dora is the administrator, and asks to refund order 4, which is 45 days old. What does she get, and why?
hint: Is the refusal about her, or about the order?

choices.text: 200, because an administrator is above the refund rule
choices.why: Nothing in orders.py exempts a role from the policy. The rule reads the order's age, not the role.

choices.text: 403, the same as Carla, because the rule is about the order
choices.why: Right. The policy is not a permission she lacks; no role changes the order's age.

choices.text: 409, because the order is shipped
choices.why: A shipped order can be refunded. 409 is for one that is already refunded or cancelled.

choices.text: 404, because the order is not hers
choices.why: She holds `orders:read_all`, so `find` returns every order to her.

prompt: An ABAC policy reads attributes of four things. Match each attribute to what it describes.
hint: `placed_on` is stored on the order.

prompt: Match each request to orders.py with the status it receives.
hint: One status is never the answer here.

pairs.left: Ana's app token placing an order

prompt: Why does orders.py answer 404, not 403, when Ana asks for Bruno's order?
hint: The ids are consecutive.

choices.text: A 403 would tell her that order 3 exists
choices.why: Right. Walking the ids and counting the 403s would count the shop's orders; a 404 tells a stranger nothing they did not send.

choices.text: Because Ana's token is not valid for that order
choices.why: Tokens are not per order; hers is valid, and a token problem would be a 401.

choices.text: Because 403 is reserved for administrative functions
choices.why: 403 is also what a missing scope and the refund policy answer.

choices.text: Because the order really is missing from her copy of the database
choices.why: There is one database, and the order is in it; `find` decides she may not see it.

prompt: The shop adds `POST /admin/reports/rebuild`, listed in its OpenAPI document, needing `reports:write`. Carla's role lacks it. Which status should she get?
hint: Is the thing being hidden an object or a function?

choices.text: 404, so that nobody learns the route exists
choices.why: The route is in the published document already. Hiding it hides nothing, and leaves Carla nothing to ask for.

choices.text: 403, naming the permission
choices.why: Right. A function in the documentation is no secret, and the refusal is something she can act on.

choices.text: 401, so that her client fetches a token with more in it
choices.why: A new token for the same person meets the same role. 401 is for not knowing who is asking.

choices.text: 405, because the method is not allowed to her
choices.why: 405 is about the address and the method, the same for every caller. Her refusal is about her.

prompt: `matrix.py` has 7 rows in `EXPECTED` and 6 endpoints. You add one more token and two more endpoints. How many checks does a run make then?
hint: Every token against every endpoint.

prompt: Put the steps that prove the matrix can catch a missing ownership check in order.
hint: The broken copy needs the port that orders.py is holding.
items: Write `broken.py` without the two lines of the check
Run `matrix.py` again and see 3 wrong, exit status 1
trap: Starting `broken.py` while `orders.py` still holds port 8000 fails, and the matrix would test the old server.

prompt: Ana's app token sends `POST /orders/2/refund`. Order 2 is Ana's. What comes back?
hint: Ask the gates in order, and ask the role before the token.

choices.text: 403 with `insufficient_scope`, because the token lacks `orders:refund`
choices.why: The token lacks it, and so does Ana's role. orders.py only blames the token when the role has the permission.

choices.text: 404, because a refund route does not show customers' orders
choices.why: The request never reaches `find`; it is refused at the permission gate.

choices.text: 200, since the order is hers and only 10 days old
choices.why: Owning the order and its age are later gates. Refunding is not a customer's function.

choices.text: 403: the role customer lacks orders:refund
choices.why: Right. Neither half grants it, and the message names the role because the role is where it was never granted.

prompt: Which of these mistakes would `matrix.py`, exactly as written, catch? Choose all that apply.
hint: It sends six requests per token and compares only the status.

choices.text: Deleting the ownership check in `find`
choices.why: Right. Three cells turned 200 when that was done.

choices.text: `show` sending `note` to customers
choices.why: The status stays 200 either way; the matrix never reads a body.

choices.text: Dropping `& scopes`, so a token gets its owner's whole role
choices.why: Right. Ana's app token would place an order: 201 where 403 is expected.

choices.text: Removing the 30-day refund rule
choices.why: No column asks for a refund, so nothing in the table depends on the rule.

prompt: No check in orders.py compares a role name. Each one asks whether a ___ is in the caller's set.
hint: Something like `orders:refund`.

prompt: Eva is given a new token carrying every scope orders.py uses. Her role is still `auditor`. What can she do now?
hint: Intersect her role's set with the token's.

choices.text: Nothing more: every request is still a 403
choices.why: Right. An unknown role grants the empty set, and the empty set intersected with anything is empty.

choices.text: Everything the token lists, since the role grants nothing to subtract
choices.why: The role is not subtracted from; it is intersected with. An empty role leaves nothing.

choices.text: Read her own orders, the one thing every role is given
choices.why: No permission is given to every role; `auditor` has no row at all.

choices.text: Only list people, like an auditor would
choices.why: The role's name means nothing to the code. Only its row in `ROLES` would, and there is none.
